question:
Patient note:
A 55-year-old man is interviewed in the ambulatory orthopedic suite just before being wheeled into theater for a brief diagnostic and therapeutic knee arthroscopy that the surgical team estimates will require less than one hour of tourniquet time under general anesthesia with possible laryngeal mask airway. The indication is a posterior horn medial meniscal tear documented on MRI after a low-speed twisting injury during a weekend pick-up basketball game; other than mild swelling after activity he has remained fully ambulatory, continues his job as a shipping-yard foreman that involves climbing ladders and walking several miles of warehouse floor daily, and rode his bicycle to work three days this week. He has had no operations or invasive procedures within the past year, and the current problem is his first orthopedic issue requiring the operating room. Medical history is notable for ileocolonic Crohn disease diagnosed in his late twenties, managed on maintenance ustekinumab every eight weeks and oral mesalamine; he has been in clinical remission for more than a year with one well-formed bowel movement daily, denies abdominal pain, hematochezia, or extraintestinal manifestations, and has not required systemic corticosteroids or hospital admission since initiation of biologic therapy. Approximately five years ago, prompted by a brother’s early myocardial infarction and the patient’s own desire to start low-dose aspirin, a hematologist performed an inherited thrombophilia panel; results revealed heterozygosity for the G20210A prothrombin gene variant, while testing for the Leiden mutation of factor V, antiphospholipid antibodies, and elevated cardiolipin titers was unremarkable. He has never experienced spontaneous leg swelling, calf tenderness, unexplained shortness of breath, or chest pain suggestive of venous or pulmonary thromboembolism, has never been told he had a clot on imaging, and has never taken long-term anticoagulation. He reports no varicose veins, wears socks that leave no indentations, and recent physical examinations by his primary physician have documented equal calf circumferences and brisk pedal pulses. There is no history of plaster casting, traction devices, pelvic or long-bone fractures, traumatic injuries, cerebrovascular accidents, spinal cord compromise, sepsis, bacterial pneumonia, or generalized inflammatory states over the last month, and he has never been admitted for heart-failure exacerbation or evaluated for orthopnea or paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea. The patient uses no indwelling vascular catheters, ports, or pumps; peripheral access this morning is a single 20-gauge cannula placed in the left antecubital fossa. Medications taken last evening include ustekinumab (administered at clinic two weeks ago), mesalamine 4 g, vitamin D 2000 IU, and a daily multivitamin; he is not on hormones, selective estrogen receptor modulators, erythropoiesis-stimulating agents, chronic glucocorticoids, or antiplatelet drugs, having decided against prophylactic aspirin once the prothrombin mutation was discovered. He stopped smoking cigarettes 15 years ago after a 10-pack-year exposure, drinks two to three glasses of red wine weekly, and denies recreational drug use. Review of systems this morning is negative for fever, chills, productive cough, wheeze, dyspnea on exertion, chest pain, palpitations, edema, weight loss, night sweats, rash, oral ulcers, ocular pain, or joint stiffness beyond the right knee symptoms already described. On examination he sits upright on the stretcher chatting comfortably with staff. Vitals: temperature 36.8 °C, blood pressure 124/72 mm Hg, heart rate 72 beats per minute and regular, respiratory rate 14 per minute, oxygen saturation 98 % on room air, and body mass index 26 kg/m². Jugular venous pulsation is not elevated, carotid upstrokes are brisk, the point of maximal impulse is mid-clavicular at the fifth interspace, S₁ and S₂ are crisp without murmurs, rubs, or gallops, and peripheral pulses are 2+ symmetrically. Lungs are clear to percussion and auscultation with full expansion. Abdomen is soft, nondistended, and nontender; healed laparoscopic scars from an appendectomy performed in adolescence are the only marks. Both lower extremities are warm and well perfused; the right knee shows a small suprapatellar effusion and mild medial joint-line tenderness but no erythema, increased heat, or calf discomfort, and Homan sign is absent bilaterally. No rope-like superficial veins, edema, or skin discoloration is observed down to the ankles. Neurologic screening demonstrates intact cranial nerves, 5/5 strength in all major muscle groups, normal sensation to light touch, and physiologic reflexes. Laboratory results drawn yesterday include hemoglobin 14.6 g/dL, hematocrit 43 %, platelets 258 × 10⁹/L, white blood cells 6.8 × 10⁹/L, sodium 139 mmol/L, potassium 4.2 mmol/L, creatinine 0.91 mg/dL, AST 20 U/L, ALT 18 U/L, total bilirubin 0.7 mg/dL, prothrombin time 12.0 s with an INR of 1.0, and activated partial thromboplastin time 29 s. Electrocardiogram on admission displays normal sinus rhythm without conduction abnormalities or ischemic changes, and a plain anteroposterior chest radiograph obtained for pre-operative clearance last week shows clear lung fields and a normal mediastinal silhouette. Airway assessment reveals Mallampati class II view, three-finger mouth opening, full cervical extension, and intact dentition; anesthesia expects straightforward mask ventilation and intubation if required. Sequential compression sleeves are present on the stretcher but remain deflated until the patient is transferred to the operating table, and no anticoagulant prophylaxis has been administered pre-incision in accordance with institutional protocol for short arthroscopic procedures.

Question: What is the patient's Caprini Score for Venous Thromboembolism?
solution:
The Caprini surgical VTE score sums weighted patient and procedure risk factors. Using the version with a BMI >30 kg/m² obesity threshold:
• Age 55 (41–60 years): 1 point.
• History of inflammatory bowel disease: 1 point for Crohn disease, even in remission.
• Planned knee arthroscopy: 2 points; do not also score minor surgery.
• Documented prothrombin G20210A thrombophilia: 3 points, even without prior VTE.
BMI 26 adds 0 under this threshold. He is ambulatory, has no prior VTE, and has no other qualifying factors. Total = 1 + 1 + 2 + 3 = 7. A Caprini version using BMI >25 would add 1 point instead.
Final answer: 7
